title: Proverbs Copied by Hezekiah's Men
summary: A new collection of Solomon's proverbs begins, copied by the scribes of King Hezekiah. It opens with sayings about God, kings, and conduct at court, then offers a gallery of comparisons drawn from weather, jewelry, food, and daily life, on words well spoken, restraint, false witness, and self-control, including the command to feed a hungry enemy.
story: With chapter 25 Proverbs turns to its fourth major section (chapters 25 to 29), a second collection of Solomon's proverbs. The heading tells us these sayings were copied, or transcribed, by the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah, more than two centuries after Solomon. So the book itself shows us wisdom being handed on: first spoken, then gathered by later scribes who judged it worth preserving for their generation. The collection begins with the king and his court and then moves into ordinary relationships with neighbors, enemies, and oneself.
historical:
Hezekiah reigned in Judah around 715 to 686 BC. The books of Kings and Chronicles remember him as a reforming king who trusted the LORD, restored temple worship, and survived the Assyrian invasion under Sennacherib in 701 BC. Scholars have often suggested that his reign saw a revival of literary activity in Jerusalem, especially after refugees arrived from the northern kingdom when Samaria fell in 722 BC. Verse 1 fits that picture: royal scribes collecting and copying older material from Solomon's era. The heading doesn't say how the proverbs had been preserved until then, whether in writing or oral tradition.

The sayings in verses 2 to 7 assume a royal court with officials, nobles, and a king whose heart is unsearchable. They reflect the world of Jerusalem's palace, where proximity to the king meant honor and a misstep could mean disgrace.
cultural:
Several comparisons draw on the climate of the land. Snow in harvest (verse 13) most likely refers to snow brought down from the mountains to cool drinks during the hot grain harvest, a luxury, or to the cold of snow imagined as refreshment; either way, it pictures relief in the heat. Rain would be unwelcome at harvest. The north wind that brings rain (verse 23) is puzzling because in Israel rain usually comes from the west, and interpreters have suggested a local wind pattern, a northwestern wind, or a proverb borrowed from another region.

Verse 24 pictures a flat roof, where people in ancient Israel slept, stored goods, and sometimes built small rooms. Living on a corner of it would be cramped and exposed. The seating customs behind verses 6 and 7 were strict: guests at a royal gathering stood or sat by rank, and taking a higher place than one's due risked public humiliation when the host moved you down.
literary: This collection favors the comparison proverb, in which two things are set side by side, often without a verb: like this, so that. Verses 11 to 14 and 18 to 20 are strings of such pictures, and verses 25 to 28 add more. The reader must work out the point of comparison: a word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver because both are beautiful and fitting. Verses 2 to 7 form a small unit on kings, and verses 6 and 7 connect with verses 8 to 10 on going to court. The chapter is framed by the idea of searching: it is the glory of kings to search out a matter (verse 2), and it is not good to search out one's own glory (verse 27).

outline.t: Heading: proverbs copied by Hezekiah's men
God, kings, and humility at court
Caution in disputes with a neighbor
Fitting words, faithful messengers, and patience
Restraint with honey and neighbors; false and faithless people
Backbiting, quarreling, good news, and self-control

doctrines.note: Wisdom here is a sense of fit: the right word at the right time, the right amount of honey, the right frequency of visits. Much of the chapter trains the reader to notice what suits a situation.
Verse 2 says it is the glory of God to conceal a matter. God is not fully knowable to human search, yet he gives understanding, and kings (and all who rule) are called to search out what is true.

The king's throne is established in righteousness when the wicked are removed from his presence (verse 5). Proverbs ties good rule to justice, a theme the prophets would press hard against Judah's kings.

words.note: Mashal, proverb. The word has a wide range: a short saying, a comparison, a parable, even a taunt song. Its root is often connected with likeness or comparison, which suits this chapter's many pictures. Here it names the whole collection that Hezekiah's men copied.

Gechel, a burning coal. Verse 22 says that feeding an enemy will heap burning coals on his head. Most interpreters take this as an image of the burning shame or remorse that kindness produces, which may lead the enemy to change. Others have proposed a background in an ancient ritual of repentance. The verse is quoted by Paul in Romans 12:20.

Satar, to hide or conceal. In verse 2 God's glory lies partly in what he conceals, and the king's glory in searching it out. The contrast teaches that human understanding, even a king's, always works within limits set by God.

Kavod, glory or honor, from a root meaning heavy or weighty. The word frames the chapter: God's glory in verse 2 and the warning against seeking one's own glory in verse 27. True honor is given, not grasped.

christ: Jesus' teaching on taking the lowest seat at a wedding feast (Luke 14:7-11) closely resembles verses 6 and 7: it is better to be invited up than to be sent down. Jesus uses this ordinary wisdom to teach the humility of God's kingdom, where those who humble themselves will be exalted. Paul quotes verses 21 and 22 in Romans 12 when he tells Christians not to take revenge but to overcome evil with good. Behind both stands Christ himself, who did not grasp at glory but humbled himself, and who died for his enemies, feeding and forgiving those who had wronged him. Proverbs gives the pattern; the gospel shows its fullest form.
questions: Verse 11 praises a word fitly spoken. Think of a time someone said the right thing to you at the right moment. What made it fitting?
What would it look like, in a specific relationship, to feed your enemy when he is hungry?
Verse 28 compares a man without self-control to a city whose walls are broken down. What does that picture suggest about the purpose of self-control?
